rationale: A wins because it keeps the facts on a leash. Its best instinct is in “not pitched as a proven result, because there are none”; B’s “A State Fire Agency Agreed to Work With a Satellite Company That Has No Satellites” is the more exciting angle, but it turns an unnamed, non-binding MOU into a procurement anomaly before proving the anomaly. B has sharper ambition; A is the set I would let a founder use with fewer chances of walking into a reporter’s buzz saw.
gaps_in_A: “Can satellites cut wildfire detection from hours to minutes?” invents the “hours” baseline. The update says minutes and faster than current systems, not what current systems take.

“launch-cadence and rocket discipline from SpaceX plus Earth-observation constellation experience from Planet Labs” assumes the founders’ actual roles and transferable expertise before those roles are confirmed.
“The founder-profile angle is the most pitchable today” may underweight the MOU. If the agency can be named and will speak, the government/public-safety angle could beat founder pedigree.
gaps_in_B: “Ex-SpaceX and Planet Labs Engineers” invents job function. The update says founders are ex-SpaceX and ex-Planet Labs, not that they were engineers.
“The Race to Spot a Wildfire From Space Before It Becomes a Disaster” dresses one startup funding round as a race. That trend needs comparables before it gets a headline.

“The prevailing assumption is that fire and public-safety agencies require demonstrated, operational capability before formalizing working agreements” is an unsupported premise. It might be true, but the update does not prove it.

“mission-aligned capital is taking disproportionate hardware risk on climate-adaptation infrastructure that return-maximizing funds won't” overreads two unnamed climate angels into an investor thesis. That is board-deck vapor until someone says it on record.
